paper_title: How Does "English (US)" Become the Default? Triangulating Structural Bias Towards American English Across the LLM Pipeline

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in educational, professional, and public infrastructure, yet widely used platforms expose "English (US)" as a primary English setting despite the global diversity of English. We ask: How does "English (US)" become the default? We study this question as structural bias, examining how geopolitical histories of data curation, digital dominance, and linguistic standardization intersect with the LLM development pipeline. Using British English as a controlled reference, we construct a curated resource of 1,813 matched American English (AmE)--British English (BrE) variants and introduce DiAlign, a dynamic, training-free method for estimating regional alignment from distributional evidence. We triangulate the AmE preference across data exposure --> representation --> generation, jointly examining pretraining and post-training data, tokenizer behavior and provenance, model prediction cost, and generated language across developer countries, prompt conditions, domains and sources, linguistic categories, and registers. AmE is consistently favored across all six audited pretraining corpora and 21 post-training datasets, is generally represented more compactly by tokenizers, and receives lower prediction cost. It also remains the dominant generation default under neutral English prompting; British-English prompting shifts this preference toward BrE but does not consistently eliminate the AmE default. To our knowledge, this is the first rigorous pipeline-wide study of structural bias across major phases of LLM development. Our findings show that contemporary LLMs privilege AmE as the de facto norm, raising concerns about linguistic homogenization, epistemic injustice, and inequity in global AI deployment, while providing a rigorous basis for targeted component-level intervention.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly expanding across technical, professional, educational, legal, and public-sector applications (Lai et al., 2024; Kulal et al., 2024; Shahzad et al., 2025; Sajadieh et al., 2026). AI is now used in at least one area of government in 35 of 36 OECD countries (OECD, 2026), while national AI strategies increasingly emphasize sovereign control over compute, data, models, and infrastructure (Reuel et al., 2025; Sajadieh et al., 2026). As LLMs become part of institutional infrastructure, their defaults can operate at global scale. Language is one such default: English remains the most effective language for interacting with many LLMs (Behzad et al., 2024), yet widely used platforms such as ChatGPT and Claude expose English (US) as primary English setting. This motivates our central question: How does English (US) become the default? If LLMs implicitly treat American English (AmE) as the default or normative form, the concern extends beyond stylistic preference to linguistic homogenization and uneven user experience worldwide (Bender et al., 2021). Answering this question requires rigorous pipeline-wide investigation that can localize the asymmetry and identify where component-level improvements should be directed. We study this problem as structural bias: systematic linguistic advantage that appears across multiple components of model development, not only in generated text. Sociolinguistic research 1 Project website: tafseer-nayeem.github.io/LLM-structural-bias 1 Preprint. Figure 1: Triangulating how English (US) becomes the default across the LLM pipeline. We trace this asymmetry across three connected stages: data exposure representation generation, using British English as the controlled reference, Ref(BrE). The study jointly examines pretraining and post-training data, tokenizer behavior and provenance, model prediction cost, and generated language. This triangulation reveals where the American English (AmE) advantage first becomes visible, whether it persists across components, and how it manifests in model outputs. Its strength and form are examined across pipeline stages, developer countries (e.g., USA, UK, China, France, Italy, and UAE), prompt conditions (e.g., default English vs. British English), domains and sources (e.g., web, books, encyclopedic text, and mixed-domain corpora), linguistic categories (e.g., orthographic vs. vocabulary contrasts), registers (e.g., formal/encyclopedic vs. informal/conversational), and alignment confidence levels. This breadth provides deeper, pipeline-level view of structural bias. shows that power and prestige shape which linguistic forms are legitimized or marginalized (Labov, 1972; 2006). In modern LLMs, these processes intersect with geopolitical histories of data curation, digital dominance, and linguistic standardization. We therefore triangulate the AmE preference to demystify the English (US) default across data exposure representation generation, covering pretraining and post-training data, tokenization and tokenizer provenance, model prediction cost, and generated language (see Figure 1). To our knowledge, this is the first systematic and rigorous pipeline-wide experimental study of structural bias across the LLM development pipeline. This pipeline begins with data. Modern LLMs are trained on massive internet-derived corpora (Dodge et al., 2021), and English accounts for roughly 5060% of global web content (Petrosyan, 2025). Its share is even higher in several documented training mixtures: approximately 92.65% for GPT-3,2 89.7% for Llama 2 (Touvron et al., 2023), and nearly 90% for Claude 2 (Anthropic, 2023). Yet the English-language Internet is itself uneven. The global reach of U.S. media, technology companies, commerce, and digital platforms has made AmE especially prominent online (Gonçalves et al., 2018). Because web-scale pretraining draws from this ecosystem, inequalities in which English forms are produced and circulated online can become inequalities in model training. These imbalances may extend beyond linguistic form, as dominant sources also encode cultural conventions, institutional practices, and perspectives that receive greater visibility in training data (Bender et al., 2021). We examine wider infrastructure question: how globally uneven data ecosystems and historically shaped linguistic standards become reflected in foundation-model infrastructure. To measure this asymmetry, we use British English as controlled reference, denoted RefBrE. AmE and BrE provide well-documented contrasts across orthography, vocabulary, grammar, writing conventions, collocations, and multi-word usage.3 The comparison is also globally meaningful. Through histories of British colonial expansion, BrE conventions became institutionally embedded in education, government, journalism, and law across many English-using contexts, including India, Nigeria, Australia, and New Zealand, among many others (Crystal, 2003; Tikly, 2016). Later U.S. economic, cultural, technological, and digital influence expanded the international reach of AmE (Calabrese et al., 2015; Gonçalves et al., 2018). These matched regional forms therefore provide measurable lens for evaluating whether AmE receives consistent advantage across the LLM pipeline. 2OpenAI GPT-3 Dataset Language Statistics (GitHub, accessed August 06, 2026) 3Representative distinctions between AmE and BrE are shown in Table 6, and more in Tables 18 and 19. Preprint. Methodologically, we ground the analysis in 1,813 matched AmERefBrE variants and introduce DIALIGN, dynamic, training-free method for estimating regional alignment from lexical, grammatical, structural, stylistic, and multi-word evidence (2.1). We evaluate three stages: 1 Data exposure, across six pretraining corpora and 21 public post-training datasets (3); 2 Representation, through tokenization, tokenizer provenance, semantic-equivalence controls, and model prediction cost (4); and 3 Generation, under neutral English and explicit British-English prompting (5). The evidence follows the same direction across all three stages. AmE is favored in all six audited pretraining corpora and all 21 post-training datasets; its forms are generally tokenized more compactly; matched RefBrE counterfactuals receive higher per-token prediction cost across all ten evaluated checkpoints under the strict equal-token-count control; and AmE remains the dominant generation default under neutral English prompting. RefBrE prompting shifts this preference, but does not consistently eliminate the AmE default. The downstream preference is therefore accompanied by upstream asymmetries in data exposure and representation, revealing pipeline-wide pattern. The framework also identifies where component-level interventions can be directed, motivating practical recommendations for corpus construction and filtering, tokenizer design and provenance auditing, post-training data selection, and model evaluation (F). We organize the investigation around three core research questions.

sections.title: Research Questions
sections.content: RQ1: Data Exposure. Where does an American English advantage appear in the data used to train and align LLMs? We audit pretraining and post-training data to measure AmE representation (3). RQ2: Representation. Does the AmE data advantage persist in tokenization and prediction cost? We examine tokenization, provenance, semantic-equivalence controls, and paired model likelihood (4). RQ3: Generation. When LLMs generate English, does American English emerge as the default? We compare neutral English and British-English prompting across different datasets and registers (5).

sections.title: 2 Methodology: Resources and Alignment
sections.content: We introduce DIALIGN, dynamic, training-free method for estimating regional alignment from contrastive distributional evidence. The method compares study variety against reference distribution; here, American English (AmE) is the study variety and British English the controlled reference, Ref(BrE). Rather than scoring documents by topic or style, it decomposes text into overlapping local spans and aggregates lexical, grammatical, structural, stylistic, and multi-word evidence. The procedure generalizes to other variety pairs with comparable reference distributions (Appendix B.6). Regional Variant Corpus. We construct curated corpus of 1,813 matched AmERef(BrE) variants for consistent analysis across the pipeline. The pairs were manually compiled from authentic linguistic references and web-based lexicons (Table 17 of Appendix) and cover orthographic and lexical differences. sections.title: 4 RQ2: Regional Representation and Prediction-Cost Asymmetry
sections.content: Our aim is to determine whether the AmE advantage observed in data exposure is also visible in how LLMs represent and predict matched regional forms. We examine two complementary levels: whether tokenizers encode AmE variants more compactly than RefBrE counterparts, and whether language models assign lower prediction cost to AmE forms in otherwise equivalent contexts. This separates tokenizer-level representational asymmetry from preference expressed by the model itself. 4.1 Tokenization: Representation Efficiency We examine how public tokenizers encode the matched AmERefBrE variants. Our primary measure is fertility, the average number of subword tokens required to encode word (Rust et al., 2021). Lower fertility indicates more compact representation as averages can obscure fragmented forms, we also measure granularity: how often variants are represented by 1, 2, or 3+ subwords. Fertility captures average encoding cost, while granularity reveals its distribution across regional forms. AmE forms are generally represented more compactly. Across the evaluated tokenizers, Table 3 and Figure 4 show that RefBrE variants require more subword tokens than matched AmE forms. The gap is largest for vocabulary contrasts, reaching = 18.72%, while orthographic gaps among AmE-favoring tokenizers range from = 2.85% to 5.42%. Granularity shows the same pattern: RefBrE forms occur more often in the 3+ token category, indicating greater long-tail fragmentation. The magnitude varies across tokenizers. Velvet slightly favors RefBrE orthographic forms (o = 0.69%); DeepSeek has the smallest vocabulary gap (v = 12.66%); and Gemma has the lowest fertility for both forms, consistent with its larger 262K-token vocabulary. The pattern is therefore more compact representation of AmE, not uniform behavior across tokenizer families. 6 Preprint. sections.title: 5 RQ3: Regional Preference in Generation
sections.content: Our goal is to determine whether the AmE advantage observed in data exposure (RQ1) and representation (RQ2) is reflected in generated language. We use DIALIGN (2.1) to measure regional alignment under neutral English prompting and explicit British-English prompting. Experimental Setup. We evaluate open-domain question answering across two contrasting registers: Natural Questions (NQ) (Kwiatkowski et al., 2019) as more formal, encyclopedic setting, and ELI5 (Fan et al., 2019) as more informal, conversational setting. To avoid lexical priming, we remove questions containing variants from the AmERef(BrE) lexicon. For each question, we generate responses under two conditions: English and British English (en-GB), requesting 50 words to keep response length comparable across models and conditions for controlled comparison. Table 4: Regional preferences in LLM generation on Natural Questions (formal) and ELI5 (informal). sections.title: 6 Related Work
sections.content: Training data audits and curation. Prior work examines how dataset composition, quality, provenance, and curation shape model behavior. Studies show that data age, coverage, and quality affect generalization (Longpre et al., 2024), while audits identify duplication, contamination, and provenance gaps in widely used corpora (Elazar et al., 2024; Longpre et al., 2025). Other work studies corpus construction (Parmar et al., 2024), registerand domain-aware sampling (Myntti et al., 2025), and reuse of filtered web data (Nguyen et al., 2025). We add within-English variation to this auditing agenda by measuring AmE representation across pretraining and post-training data. Tokenization and representation. Tokenization can encode systematic differences before generation begins. Prior work documents substantial variation in tokenization efficiency across languages, with consequences for sequence length, context capacity, and inference cost (Petrov et al., 2023; Rust et al., 2021; Ahia et al., 2023; Ali et al., 2024). Related studies connect tokenization to demographic bias (An & Rudinger, 2023), lexical fragility (Gallifant et al., 2024), and gender bias in machine translation (Iluz et al., 2023). We study this problem within English by combining tokenization efficiency, tokenizer provenance, and paired model likelihood for matched AmE and Ref(BrE) forms. English variation in NLP and LLMs. Research on African American English (AAE), South Asian Englishes (SAsE), and other English varieties has shown systematic disparities in tagging, classification, sentiment analysis, robustness, and model behavior (Jørgensen et al., 2016; Blodgett et al., 2016; Kiritchenko & Mohammad, 2018; Ziems et al., 2023; Hofmann et al., 2024; Fleisig et al., 2024; Holt et al., 2024). We focus on different question: how an American-English default appears across the LLM pipeline. By linking training data, tokenization and prediction cost, and generation, our analysis treats regional preference as structural property that can be observed across multiple stages of model development. An extended discussion is provided in Appendix G. 9 Preprint.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: This paper presents the first rigorous pipeline-wide study of structural bias across phases of LLM development. By triangulating pretraining and post-training data, tokenizer behavior and provenance, model prediction cost, and generated language, we show that American English receives an advantage across data exposure, representation, and generation, emerging as the de facto default. These findings show how linguistic asymmetries persist across the LLM pipeline, raising concerns about linguistic homogenization, epistemic injustice, and inequity in global AI deployment, while providing basis for targeted, component-level improvements toward more inclusive language technologies.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: This work studies structural linguistic bias across the LLM development pipeline. It involves no human subjects, private user data, or sensitive personal attributes. Our analyses use publicly available pretraining and post-training datasets for research purposes (Appendix C.1). The curated AmE RefBrE resource was compiled from publicly accessible linguistic and web-based sources  (Table 17)  and contains no personal or proprietary material. We plan to release it for non-commercial research under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license.5 The ethical motivation is to understand where linguistic advantage becomes visible, persists, and manifests across data exposure, representation, and generation. Such defaults can shape which regional forms receive greater visibility as LLMs are deployed across diverse national and institutional contexts, with implications for linguistic homogenization and unequal representation. British English is used solely as controlled reference for measuring the American English preference; neither variety is treated as intrinsically superior, more correct, or more appropriate. Developer country and tokenizer provenance are likewise analyzed descriptively and are not interpreted as evidence of intent, nationality, or regional causation. The pipeline-wide audit and DIALIGN are intended for responsible regional-language auditing and for identifying where targeted improvements may be most effective. DIALIGN excludes spans containing named entities such as people, organizations, and locations, reducing privacy and reputational risks from such signals. The framework can be extended beyond AmERef(BrE) when suitable regional reference distributions and linguistic resources are available. Scope, limitations, and risks of binary regional comparison are discussed in Appendix I.

sections.content: A.1 Construction and Filtering We construct curated resource of 1,813 matched AmERef(BrE) variants for consistent measurement across the three research questions [RQ1 (Section 3), RQ2 (Section 4), and RQ3 (Section 5)]. The resource contains 1,538 orthographic pairs and 275 vocabulary pairs. Variant pairs were manually compiled from linguistic references and web-based lexicons  (Table 17)  . We merge entries across sources, normalize their representation, and remove duplicates before applying strict matching criterion. For analyses requiring direct word-level comparison, we retain one-to-one mappings in which each AmE form corresponds to one Ref(BrE) form. This criterion gives the resource common unit of analysis across corpus frequency counts, tokenizer segmentation, and paired prediction-cost experiments. Multi-word and structurally different constructions remain important for regional variation, but are handled separately by DIALIGN, whose local n-gram analysis is not restricted to the one-to-one lexicon. DIALIGN: Implementation, Validation, and Generalization B.1 Implementation Details This section records the implementation choices used for the DIALIGN experiments in the paper. Parameterization. We use the following configuration: n-gram range: {2, 3, 4, 5}. This range captures multi-word and structural evidence while remaining within the maximum order supported by Google Books Ngram. Temporal range: [ymin, ymax] = [1950, 2022]. The broader window provides stable frequency estimates across low-frequency constructions. contemporary-window analysis is reported in Section B.5. Smoothing: 0. We use the normalized yearly frequencies returned by the reference corpus without additional smoothing. Lexicon boost: β = 1.5, applied when retained span contains an entry from the curated regional variant lexicon. Frequency Lookup. For every retained span, we query the American English corpus (ID 17) and British English corpus (ID 6) in Google Books Ngram using the requests library (Lin et al., 2012). The service returns normalized yearly frequencies relative to the size of each corpus for that year. We average these normalized values over the selected temporal range. Queries are case-insensitive and use exponential-backoff retries for transient failures. persistent cache stores every queried (n-gram, corpus) pair, so repeated spans reuse previously retrieved frequencies. This substantially reduces reference-side queries when scoring large collections. Filtering. We remove spans that are likely to reflect topic or named entities rather than regional usage. candidate is discarded if it contains person, organization, or location identified through NLTK named-entity chunking, or if every token in the span is stopword.6 The resulting evidence consists of local constructions whose relative frequencies differ across the two reference distributions. These local signals are then combined with the divergence weighting and lexicon boost defined in Section 2.1. 6https://www.nltk.org 22 Preprint. Figure 6: Illustrative walkthrough of DIALIGN. Parallel AmE and Ref(BrE) passages contain matched contrasts in spelling, vocabulary, grammar, conventions, and multi-word usage. DIALIGN decomposes each passage into overlapping 25-gram candidate spans, filters non-diagnostic spans, and compares the retained constructions against the American English (ID 17) and British English (ID 6) Google Books reference corpora. The resulting local evidence is aggregated into the regional alignment scores (PAmE, PRefBrE ). B.3 Meta-evaluation Benchmark We evaluate DIALIGN on balanced set of 1,500 short news passages with strong source provenance: 750 AmE samples and 750 Ref(BrE) samples. 23 Preprint. Ref(BrE) Samples. We use English summaries from XL-Sum (Hasan et al., 2021), which is sourced from BBC News.7 We select entries whose identifiers begin with uk-englandand randomly sample 750 summaries. AmE Samples. We use the News Category Dataset (Misra, 2022), built from HuffPost articles. From the U.S. NEWS category, we randomly sample 750 short_description fields.8 Benchmark Statistics. The benchmark is therefore exactly balanced by reference variety. AmE passages contain 34.4 words on average and Ref(BrE) passages contain 24.7 words on average. The labels are based on editorial provenance rather than separate sentence-level human annotation. BBC and HuffPost also differ in editorial style and topic distribution, so we treat the benchmark as source-provenance validation set. Importantly, DIALIGN does not score passages as whole documents: it decomposes each text into overlapping local 25-gram spans, removes named-entity and stopword-only spans, and aggregates the retained contrastive evidence. This design limits reliance on document-level topic, source identity, and global stylistic differences, while the benchmark tests whether local linguistic patterns track the expected regional convention. sections.title: F Discussion and Practical Recommendations
sections.content: The AmE advantage appears consistently across data exposure, representation, and generation. RQ1 shows AmE overrepresentation in both pretraining and post-training resources, RQ2 identifies corresponding asymmetries in tokenization and model prediction cost, and RQ3 shows that AmE remains the dominant generation default under neutral English prompting. These findings suggest that regional imbalance should be addressed across the LLM development pipeline rather than only through output-level correction. Audit and Rebalance Training Data. RQ1 (3) shows that regional skew is already present in both pretraining and post-training data. Dataset construction can therefore track regional English variation alongside conventional measures of domain, quality, and language composition. For web-scale resources, provenance signals such as publisher location, institutional metadata, source URLs, and country-code top-level domains can support regional sampling strategies. For example, .uk, .in, .ng, .au, and .sg can provide useful regional signals when combined with source and publisher metadata rather than being treated as linguistic labels on their own. The same audit should extend beyond pretraining. Instruction-tuning, preference, reward-model, and safety datasets can introduce additional regional skew after pretraining. Variant-frequency counts provide lightweight way to monitor explicit spelling and vocabulary differences, while DIALIGN can complement them with broader grammatical, structural, collocational, and multi-word evidence (2.1). These diagnostics can be applied before training to compare candidate mixtures and adjust sampling when strong unintended imbalance is present. Include Regional Coverage in Tokenizer Design. RQ2 (4) shows that Ref(BrE) forms are generally segmented less compactly than matched AmE forms. Tokenizer evaluation can therefore include regional coverage alongside aggregate compression metrics. Fertility and granularity provide simple diagnostics for identifying forms that are repeatedly split into longer subword sequences. 35 Preprint. When such gaps are large, vocabulary extension or tokenizer retraining can increase coverage of underrepresented variants (Tejaswi et al., 2024). For example, forms that consistently fall into the 3+ subword category while their matched AmE counterparts are encoded more compactly are natural candidates for closer inspection. Tokenizer provenance should also be considered before reuse, since our lineage analysis shows that segmentation behavior can persist across model families through inherited tokenizer artifacts. Evaluate Prediction Cost Beyond Tokenization. More balanced segmentation does not necessarily imply equal model preference. Our controlled likelihood analysis shows that Ref(BrE) counterfactuals receive higher prediction cost even when sentence token count is identical. practical regional evaluation can therefore report both tokenization differences and loss. For example, model may tokenize color and colour using the same number of sentence tokens while still assigning the Ref(BrE) counterfactual higher per-token negative log-likelihood. Evaluating both quantities helps distinguish tokenizer-level representation from preferences encoded in the model itself. Repeating the same evaluation for base and post-trained checkpoints can also reveal whether the regional gap becomes larger or smaller across model development. Treat Regional Prompting as Steering. RQ3 shows that explicit British-English prompting generally moves outputs toward Ref(BrE), but the size of the shift varies across models and registers. Regional prompting is therefore useful as an interface control, but it should not replace upstream data and representation audits. Evaluation should also go beyond simple spelling substitution. response may use colour instead of color while still following AmE preferences in vocabulary, grammar, conventions, or multi-word usage. Regional settings should therefore be evaluated across several types of variation rather than judged only by small set of visible lexical changes. Use DIALIGN for Regional Auditing. DIALIGN can support these checks during both data construction and generation evaluation. During corpus building, it can estimate the regional alignment of candidate training data or synthetic additions. During evaluation, it can compare neutral-English and region-specific generations using the same local evidence. The framework is also adaptable beyond the present AmERef(BrE) comparison. For example, an AmEIndian English analysis could construct regional reference corpus using Indian news, institutional websites, and reliable provenance signals such as .in, combined with publisher and source-location metadata. Similar strategies could support studies of Nigerian, Australian, New Zealand, or Singapore English (Appendix B.6). These recommendations map directly to the stages examined in this paper: audit regional exposure in training data, measure asymmetry in tokenization and model prediction cost, and evaluate the realized generation default. Study limitations and directions for extending the analysis are discussed in Appendix I.

sections.title: G Extended Related Work
sections.content: Training data audits and curation. The composition of training data has substantial effects on model behavior and generalization. The Pretrainers Guide isolates the influence of data age, domain coverage, quality, and toxicity (Longpre et al., 2024), while corpus audits have exposed duplication, benchmark contamination, low-quality content, and gaps in provenance. WIMBD, for example, audits C4 and RedPajama for contamination and undesirable content (Elazar et al., 2024), and Data Portraits develops membership-testing tools for tracing training data (Marone & Durme, 2023). Broader analyses also document provenance imbalances across text, speech, and video resources, including heavy reliance on web-crawled and Western-centric sources (Longpre et al., 2025). parallel line of work studies how training corpora can be constructed and selected more effectively. This includes practical recipes for trillion-token datasets (Parmar et al., 2024), LLM-assisted quality selection through QuRating (Wettig et al., 2024), register-aware sampling (Myntti et al., 2025), domain-based organization of web text (Wettig et al., 2025), and reuse of filtered web content (Nguyen et al., 2025). Our analysis adds within-English variation to this auditing perspective by measuring 36 Preprint. AmE representation across pretraining and post-training resources and following the same directional asymmetry into later stages of the pipeline. Tokenization and representational asymmetry. Tokenization determines how linguistic forms are mapped into the discrete units consumed by language models. Prior work documents large disparities in subword segmentation across languages and scripts (Nayeem et al., 2025), with consequences for sequence length, effective context capacity, latency, and monetary cost (Petrov et al., 2023; Alqahtani et al., 2026). Tokenization length and corpus frequency can also correlate with demographic properties of personal names, disproportionately fragmenting underrepresented forms (An & Rudinger, 2023). Related robustness studies show that lexical alternations, such as brand and generic drug names, can produce substantial variation in model behavior (Gallifant et al., 2024). Other work examines the mechanisms and mitigation of such disparities. In machine translation, training distributions and subword segmentation can jointly disadvantage female and non-stereotypical gender inflections, while targeted token-embedding adaptation can reduce these gaps (Iluz et al., 2023). Controlled interventions further show that changing word from multi-token representation to single token can substantially alter its probability (Lesci et al., 2025). Parity-Aware Byte-Pair Encoding similarly trades small amount of compression for more balanced token counts across languages (Foroutan et al., 2025). Our analysis examines the same representational layer within English through tokenization efficiency, tokenizer provenance, and paired prediction cost. English variation in NLP and LLMs. Research on language variation has documented systematic performance differences across regional and social varieties of English, particularly African American English (AAE) and South Asian Englishes (SAsE) (Demszky et al., 2021; Holt et al., 2024; Joshi et al., 2025). For AAE, disparities have been reported in part-of-speech tagging (Jørgensen et al., 2016), language identification (Blodgett et al., 2016), sentiment analysis (Kiritchenko & Mohammad, 2018), dependency parsing (Blodgett et al., 2018), hate-speech detection (Sap et al., 2019), and natural-language understanding (Ziems et al., 2022). Recent studies also show that LLMs can reproduce negative stereotypes associated with AAE (Hofmann et al., 2024; Fleisig et al., 2024). User-centered studies report that SAsE speakers encounter lower reliability for their linguistic usage (Holt et al., 2024), while Multi-VALUE evaluates models across many English varieties and linguistic features, revealing broad robustness gaps (Ziems et al., 2023). Even differences between standardized English conventions affect model behavior: retrieval performance decreases when queries and documents use different spelling conventions (Chari et al., 2023), and language models respond differently to observed and novel spelling variants (Nielsen et al., 2023). Our study places the American-English default within this literature on linguistic variation, but follows it across the development pipeline rather than single downstream task. We examine its prevalence in pretraining and post-training data, its expression in tokenization and model prediction cost, and its realization in generations. This pipeline-level analysis provides common empirical view of how the same AmE advantage recurs across data exposure, representation, and generation.

sections.title: H Brief Historical Context
sections.content: The divergence between American English (AmE) and British English (BrE) reflects both deliberate standardization and broader historical change. Samuel Johnsons 1755 dictionary helped codify spelling conventions that became influential in British literary and educational practice. In the United States, Noah Websters 1828 dictionary promoted distinct and often simplified spellings as part of an emerging American linguistic identity (Baker, 2017). These processes established many of the orthographic contrasts still visible today. The two standards subsequently acquired international reach through distinct geopolitical trajectories. British colonial expansion embedded BrE conventions in administration, education, journalism, and law across Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and the Pacific. These conventions often persisted after political independence and remain institutionally influential across much of the Commonwealth and in English-using contexts such as India, Nigeria, Singapore, Australia, and New Zealand (Figure 14) (Calabrese et al., 2015; Tikly, 2016; Phillipson, 2018). This institutional footprint also persists through UK-linked language and educational institutions, including the British Council and international English assessment through IELTS. 37 Preprint. Figure 14: Timeline of independence across countries formerly under British colonization. The map highlights the wave of decolonization in the mid-twentieth century, when nations in Africa, Asia, the Caribbean, and the Pacific gained sovereignty. This geopolitical shift marked the decline of direct colonial governance but reinforced the institutional legacy of British English (BrE) in education, government, journalism, and law across many of these regions (Tikly, 2016; Phillipson, 2018). American English expanded especially rapidly during the twentieth century through U.S. economic influence, mass media and global entertainment, technological development, and global commerce (Crystal, 2003; Gonçalves et al., 2018; Nordquist, 2024). Hollywood, popular culture, digital platforms, and technology ecosystems further strengthened its international visibility, particularly in contemporary online communication. This history makes the AmEBrE contrast useful for controlled analysis. Both are extensively documented standard varieties with systematic differences across spelling, vocabulary, grammar, conventions, and multi-word usage. BrE also provides meaningful reference for institutional norms inherited by several other English varieties, while AmE has become especially prominent in the digital ecosystem from which modern LLMs are trained. Google Books provides separate reference corpora for the two varieties, allowing DIALIGN to measure regional alignment beyond the curated one-to-one variant inventory. Scope, Limitations, and Future Directions Our experiments use controlled comparisons designed to isolate the American-English advantage across multiple stages of the LLM pipeline. This design supports high-precision, cross-stage evidence and defines clear directions for broader generalization. Reference Variety and Broader English Variation. We use Ref(BrE) as controlled, globally meaningful comparator because it provides systematic contrasts with AmE across spelling, vocabulary, grammar, and usage that can be carried consistently from corpus statistics through tokenization, prediction cost, and generation. This prioritizes direct cross-stage comparability while providing template for broader regional analysis. The same pipeline can be extended to Indian, Nigerian, Singapore, Australian, New Zealand, and other English varieties when suitable reference resources are available. Appendix B.6 describes how DIALIGN can be instantiated with alternative corpora. Lexicon Precision and Coverage. The 1,813-pair resource is designed for high-precision one-toone comparison, which is especially important for tokenizer and counterfactual likelihood experiments where both regional forms must be directly comparable. We complement this resource with DIALIGN, which captures grammatical, structural, collocational, stylistic, and multi-word evidence beyond the fixed lexicon. RQ1 uses type-level corpus counts for curated variants, with context-sensitive cases Preprint. removed when they materially affect interpretation. Contextual modeling of larger web-scale variant inventories provides direct extension. Reference Corpora and Meta-evaluation. Google Books provides separate American and British English distributions, making it consistent contrastive reference for DIALIGN. Normalized regional frequencies allow direct comparison of the same local constructions across the two reference distributions. DIALIGN decomposes each input into overlapping 25-gram spans and aggregates retained contrastive evidence at the local level. The resulting signal generalizes across domains: DIALIGN reaches 93.18% accuracy on the external BBCHuffPost news benchmark, shows the same directional AmE pattern across encyclopedic, web, and mixed-domain pretraining corpora, and extends to model-generated open-domain responses in RQ3. Separately, the 2000-2022 robustness analysis yields nearly identical performance to the 1950-2022 setting, demonstrating temporal stability of the regional contrast. matched-domain benchmark with independently annotated variety labels would further broaden evaluation across source conditions. Generation Setting. RQ3 uses two contrasting open-domain registers under fixed responselength protocol to isolate regional preference while controlling generation length. Natural Questions provides more formal, encyclopedic setting, while ELI5 provides more conversational one, and the observed preference is stable to realized response length (Section E.5). Long-form dialogue, specialized professional domains, mixed-variety inputs, and creative generation provide natural extensions for testing the default under more complex discourse and user contexts. Tokenizer and Checkpoint Coverage. Our tokenizer panel spans multiple model families, vocabulary sizes, and development contexts, while the provenance audit separates independent tokenizers from inherited infrastructure. Prediction-cost experiments focus on five model families with matched public base and post-trained checkpoints, prioritizing within-family comparability over nominal model count. Larger closed models and families without comparable public checkpoints remain represented where artifact access permits, including tokenizer and generation experiments. Attribution Across Pipeline Stages. The study traces where recurring AmE asymmetry becomes visible across data exposure, tokenization, prediction cost, and generation. The consistency across these stages establishes structural pattern. Causal decomposition requires controlled interventions such as retraining with rebalanced data, tokenizer replacement, or matched post-training interventions, providing natural next step from structural tracing to causal attribution. 39 Preprint.
